claims.text: Welcome to Palais Lascaris, a captivating museum nestled in the heart of Nice, France, dedicated to the evolution of musical instruments and their profound influence on European music culture.

As you explore this remarkable collection, you will encounter four exquisite works: the Violes gambe by William Turner, the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, the Harpe by Naderman, and the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer.

The Palais Lascaris, bequeathed to the city of Nice in a testament dated 1901, houses this extraordinary collection, including one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in original condition by Anton Schnitzer, and Turner's Violes gambe, often played in concert within the palace's salon.
This exhibition, opened to the public in 2011, offers a rare glimpse into the historical musical instrument collections of Nice, transferred from the Musee Massena to this splendid venue.
Your first stop is Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652).
Stand in the intimate salon of the Palais Lascaris, where the light dapples through antique windows, casting a warm glow on the six-string bass viola da gamba crafted by William Turner in 1652.
This positioning allows you to appreciate the intricate heart-shaped ornament carved on the back of the pegbox scroll, a signature of Turner's craftsmanship.
In 1652, the English luthier William Turner created this six-string bass viola da gamba in London.
Its distinctive feature—a heart-shaped ornament carved into the pegbox scroll—exemplifies Turner's attention to detail and artistic vision.

This generous act ensured its preservation and public accessibility at the Palais Lascaris, a former aristocratic residence now home to France's second most significant collection of musical instruments, only surpassed by the Musée de la Musique in Paris.
Its presence in the Palais Lascaris is a poignant reminder of the rich musical dialogues that transcended national borders.

The intricate heart-shaped design on the pegbox scroll is a signature element found in many of Turner's creations, underscoring the artistic flair and innovation that marked his contributions to lutherie.

claims.text: This bass viol, measuring 1,445 mm in total length, showcases the intricate design that made Milanese instruments a staple in European orchestras.
As you stand here, admire the fine details of the Harpe by Naderman, crafted in Paris around 1780.
Position yourself to observe its ornate carvings and gilded embellishments, capturing the exquisite finesse associated with Jean-Henri Naderman's work.
Jean-Henri Naderman, renowned for his craftsmanship, built this harp to serve the opulent tastes of the French aristocracy.
He was originally appointed harp maker in ordinary to Queen Marie-Antoinette in 1778 by crafting unparalleled instruments that elevated the harp's status in French courts.
The harp itself, standing at an impressive 161.5 centimeters, is crafted from fine wood and adorned with various materials, echoing the aesthetic sensibilities of 18th-century France.
At Palais Lascaris, the harp connects to a broader narrative of musical evolution, complementing pieces like the basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore from 1696.
Stand before the sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in 1581, and note the meticulously engraved bell garland bearing Schnitzer's name and the year, a testament to its enduring history.
Schnitzer, a renowned craftsman of the Nuremberg tradition, specialized in creating ceremonial brass instruments, and this sacqueboute exemplifies his skill.
The refined engravings and structural integrity speak to the Schnitzer family's legacy in brass instrument craftsmanship.

Just as the harp by Naderman you saw earlier reveals the evolution of string instruments, this piece offers insight into the progression of brass instruments, setting the stage for the development of the modern trombone.
